newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Looming election heats up JGB risk.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Looming election heats up JGB risk.

text.p: Political uncertainty ahead of general elections on October 20 will keep overseas investors out of Japanese government bonds (JGBs), despite the recent rally, analysts said on Tuesday.
Even once the election has passed, analysts said rate hike speculation will prevent funds from moving into the market.

"Political agitation going into the election is leading to a lot of rate and currency statements," said Sean Shepley, international economist at CS First Boston in London. "As that has risen, the surge of interest in JGBs has died away."

The election is for the 500-seat Lower House, and is the first since July 1993. Since it was called in September, markets have been buzzing with speculation over when rock-bottom interest rates would rise, fueled by reports of statements from senior government officials.

Earlier on Tuesday, JGBs rallied after a newswire reported Eisukie Sakakibara, director general of the Japanese Finance Ministry's international bureau, said rates were unlikely to be raised until at least the end of the fiscal year ending March 31. Sakakibara later denied the comments and JGBs retreated from highs.
The Japanese official discount rate is currently at 0.50 percent.

"We are particularly wary of the short end, and consider the five- to ten-year area much safer," said Peter Frank, senior economist at Sumitomo Finance International in London. "But right now the ten-year area is so expensive, nowhere is safe."
Shepley said foreign investors were worried that unhedged JGB positions were vulnerable to currency risks, and they were likely to remain underweight of the market.

Analysts said beyond the election the main uncertainty was the rate outlook for Japan. The market is still on the lookout for a 25 basis point hike in the ODR, although speculation about the timing varies considerably.
Frank said the recent rally has left the market expensive, although there was no sign of a trigger for prices to push lower.
December JGB futures in Tokyo set a contract high of 122.60 on September 26, after ralling from a low of 116.75 on July 17. They were at 122.14 by 1144 GMT.
The yield on the benchmark 182nd 10-year JGB stood at 2.820 percent by the same time.
Frank said investors wishing to get into the market should look for a re-entry point at a yield of 3.0 to 3.20 percent on the 182nd bond.
"Most funds have been underweight all year and we're saying to them that now is not the time to move in," he said. "But if the yield goes above 3.0 percent then they should move to neutral."
On a spread basis, Shepley said he expected some outperformance by JGBs over U.S. Treasuries as U.S. bonds continued to suffer from interest rate anxiety.
"The spread could go to 375 or 360 basis points by the year end," he said. The spread was at 398 points by 1100 GMT.
Peter Wilson, strategist at Tokyo Mitsubishi in London, said the market could push higher, despite the recent rally.
"The upward price action is very strong and any dips immediately bore the market," he said. "The four-year auction was well-covered at 3.04 times so that suggests that people want the bonds."
Japan auctioned 500 billon yen worth of 1.7 percent four-year government notes.
Wilson said he advised British funds to hold some JGBs, but to hedge the currency risk. "Hedged JGBs are dollar currency risk," he said. "There is no exposure to yen weakness."
